title: Polymers, Bonding and Materials
description: Choosing materials and how their structure explains their properties.
hero_image_caption: Every polymer tells a structural story — the way its chains link, fold and interact determines whether the material bends, snaps, melts or endures.
content_html:
From Monomers to Polymers

A polymer is a very large molecule formed by linking many small molecules called monomers together. The properties of a polymer depend on the type of monomer, how the chains are arranged, and how strongly they interact with each other. Choosing the right polymer for a job requires understanding these structure–property relationships.

Key Fact

Monomer: small molecule with reactive sites. Polymer: very large molecule formed by linking many monomers. Two types of polymerisation: addition (monomers with C=C, no by-product) and condensation (monomers with two functional groups, releases water or HCl as by-product).

Addition Polymerisation

Addition polymerisation occurs when alkene monomers react together. The \(C=C\) double bond in each monomer opens up, and the monomers join in a long chain. No atoms are lost — the polymer contains all the atoms of the original monomers.

Important examples of addition polymers and their uses:

  • Poly(ethene) — from ethene (\(CH_2=CH_2\)): flexible, low density → carrier bags, packaging film.
  • Poly(propene) — from propene (\(CH_3CH=CH_2\)): tougher, higher density → crates, ropes, car parts.
  • Poly(chloroethene) / PVC — from chloroethene: rigid form for pipes; plasticised form for cable insulation.
  • Poly(tetrafluoroethene) / PTFE — from tetrafluoroethene: very low friction, non-stick → cookware coatings.

The equation for addition polymerisation is written using a bracket with the repeating unit and the letter \(n\) to indicate that the unit repeats many times. For poly(ethene):

$$n\,CH_2=CH_2 \rightarrow [-CH_2-CH_2-]_n$$

The lines extending beyond the brackets show that the chain continues. To go from the monomer to the repeating unit: remove the double bond and show single bonds extending left and right. To go from the repeating unit to the monomer: put the double bond back in.

Condensation Polymerisation

Condensation polymerisation is different from addition polymerisation in two important ways: the monomers must have two reactive groups (one at each end), and a small molecule — typically water — is released at each bond formed. The polymer chain and the by-product are produced simultaneously.

Key examples:

  • Polyesters — formed from a diol (two –OH groups) and a dicarboxylic acid (two –COOH groups). The linkage formed is an ester bond (–COO–). Water is released at each bond.
  • Polyamides (nylons) — formed from a diamine (two –NH₂ groups) and a dicarboxylic acid (two –COOH groups). The linkage formed is an amide bond (–NHCO–). Water is released at each bond.

PET (polyethylene terephthalate) is formed from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, releasing water at each ester bond. It is strong, transparent, and suitable for food contact — which is why it is used for fizzy drink bottles. PET is also spun into polyester fibres for clothing and carpets. It can be recycled — old bottles can be reprocessed into new ones or into fibre fill for jackets.

The choice of PET over glass or aluminium for drinks bottles illustrates a real materials decision: PET is lighter (reducing transport energy), cheaper to produce, shatterproof, and recyclable. However, its persistence in the environment if not properly recycled is a significant disadvantage — a key consideration in a life-cycle assessment.

Thermosoftening and Thermosetting Polymers

The relationship between a polymer's structure and its thermal properties determines how it can be used and how it is processed.

Thermosoftening polymers (thermoplastics) have long polymer chains held together only by weak intermolecular forces. When heated, these forces are overcome and the chains can slide past each other — the polymer softens and can be remoulded. When cooled, the intermolecular forces reform and the shape is retained. This makes thermoplastics recyclable — they can be melted and reshaped repeatedly. Examples: poly(ethene), poly(propene), PET, PVC.

Thermosetting polymers have polymer chains that are joined by strong covalent cross-links. These cross-links form during the initial moulding and are permanent. Heating does not soften the polymer — instead, enough heat will cause it to char or burn. This makes thermosets non-recyclable but gives them excellent heat resistance and structural rigidity. Examples: epoxy resin, Bakelite, melamine (used in electrical sockets, saucepan handles, worktops).

Key Fact

Thermosoftening: chains held by weak intermolecular forces → softens on heating → recyclable. Examples: poly(ethene), PET. Thermosetting: chains joined by covalent cross-links → does not soften → non-recyclable. Examples: epoxy resin, Bakelite (electrical plugs, saucepan handles).

Choosing Materials — Structure Governs Properties

The key principle in materials science is that structure determines properties. When a designer or engineer selects a material, they are really choosing the molecular or atomic arrangement that will deliver the required physical and chemical properties. For polymers, the key questions are: is it addition or condensation? Thermosoftening or thermosetting? How tightly are the chains packed? Are there cross-links?

When scientists and engineers evaluate materials, they do not simply look for the 'best' material — they weigh up competing factors: cost, availability, durability, environmental impact, safety, and recyclability. This is the kind of risk–benefit thinking (IaS4) that is central to materials science and to this specification. PET bottles are lighter and shatterproof but create plastic waste if not collected. Thermosetting polymers resist heat but cannot be recovered after use. No material is ideal in all respects.

Life-cycle assessment (LCA) is a tool scientists use to compare the total environmental impact of different material choices across their whole life cycle — from raw material extraction and manufacturing, through use, to disposal or recycling. An LCA of a PET bottle versus a glass bottle, for instance, would consider energy use at every stage, not just the end-of-life scenario.
exam_tip_html: For questions on addition vs condensation polymerisation, the key distinguishing fact is whether a small molecule (water) is released — if yes, it is condensation. For thermosoftening vs thermosetting, always explain in terms of bonding: intermolecular forces (thermosoftening) vs covalent cross-links (thermosetting). When asked to evaluate materials choices, use risk–benefit language: identify advantages and disadvantages for each option and reach a reasoned conclusion — don't just list facts.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Addition polymers form when alkene monomers open their C=C double bonds to join in a chain with no by-product. Condensation polymers form from monomers with two functional groups, releasing water at each linkage (e.g. PET from diol + dicarboxylic acid).
  • Thermosoftening polymers have chains held by weak intermolecular forces — they soften on heating and are recyclable. Thermosetting polymers have covalent cross-links — they cannot soften or be recycled but offer excellent heat resistance.
  • Structure determines properties. Choosing a material requires weighing cost, performance, environmental impact and recyclability — a risk–benefit decision that sits at the heart of materials science.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a correct statement about addition polymerisation?
A) A small molecule (e.g. water) is released at each bond
B) The monomer must have two functional groups
C) The monomer must contain a C=C double bond
D) The product is always a polyamide
practice_questions.marks: C) The monomer must contain a C=C double bond [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the type of bond formed when thermosetting polymers are heated and explain why they cannot be reshaped.
practice_questions.marks: Thermosetting polymers have covalent cross-links between chains [1]; these cross-links are permanent — heating cannot break them, so the chains cannot slide and the polymer cannot be reshaped [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe the differences between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. In your answer, refer to the monomers needed and whether any by-product is formed.
practice_questions.marks: Addition: monomers must contain a C=C double bond [1]; chains join with no by-product formed [1]. Condensation: monomers must have two functional groups (e.g. –OH and –COOH) [1]; a small molecule (usually water) is released at each bond formed [1]. (Max 3 marks.)

practice_questions.text: PET is used for fizzy drink bottles. Explain the structure of PET, name the type of monomers used to make it, and compare it with a thermosetting polymer in terms of thermal properties and recyclability.
practice_questions.marks: PET is a polyester [1]; made from a diol (ethylene glycol) and a dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid) by condensation polymerisation [1]; it is a thermosoftening polymer — can be melted and reshaped / recycled [1]; unlike thermosetting polymers which have covalent cross-links and cannot soften or be recycled [1].

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer must choose between a thermosoftening polymer and a thermosetting polymer to make the handle of an electric saucepan that will reach temperatures above 100 °C. Evaluate which polymer is more appropriate, giving reasons for your choice and acknowledging a limitation of the chosen material.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: thermosetting is more appropriate for a saucepan handle [1]; because it has covalent cross-links that do not break at high temperatures [1]; it will not soften or deform when heated above 100 °C [1]; in contrast, a thermosoftening polymer would soften when heated, making it unsafe [1]; limitation: thermosetting cannot be recycled after use because the cross-links are permanent [1]; the manufacturer should consider this environmental disadvantage in a full life-cycle assessment [1]. Secure: four points with clear evaluation. Developing: correctly identifies thermosetting and gives one structural reason.

practice_questions.text: Write the repeat unit for poly(propene) and explain, in terms of bonding changes, how the monomer propene (CH₃–CH=CH₂) is converted to the polymer during addition polymerisation.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: correct repeat unit drawn or written: –[CH₂–CH(CH₃)]ₙ– [1]; in addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond in each propene monomer opens [1]; one bond of the double bond breaks [1]; the resulting reactive sites on adjacent monomers form new C–C single bonds [1]; building the chain; no atoms are lost — the empirical formula of the repeat unit is the same as the monomer [1]. Secure: four points. Developing: identifies C=C opens and chain forms.

knowledge_checks.q: What type of bond is broken when an alkene monomer undergoes addition polymerisation?
What small molecule is released during the formation of a polyester?
Which type of polymer can be recycled by melting and remoulding: _____
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Thermosoftening polymer.

knowledge_checks.q: What structural feature prevents thermosetting polymers from softening when heated: _____
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Covalent cross-links between chains.

knowledge_checks.explanation: Review the key terms and definitions covered in this lesson.

flashcard_questions.a: Polymerisation in which alkene monomers open their C=C double bond and join in a long chain with no by-product formed.
Polymerisation in which monomers with two functional groups react together, releasing a small molecule (usually water) at each bond formed.

flashcard_questions.q: What is PET and how is it made?
flashcard_questions.a: Polyethylene terephthalate — a polyester made by condensation polymerisation of a diol (ethylene glycol) and a dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid), releasing water at each ester bond.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can thermosoftening polymers be recycled but thermosetting polymers cannot?
flashcard_questions.a: Thermosoftening: chains held by weak intermolecular forces that break on heating — can be melted and remoulded. Thermosetting: covalent cross-links that do not break — cannot be reshaped.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two uses of thermosetting polymers and explain why a thermosoftening polymer would not work in these applications.
flashcard_questions.a: Electrical sockets and saucepan handles — both involve heat. A thermosoftening polymer would soften at these temperatures, creating a safety hazard.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'structure determines properties' mean in materials science?
flashcard_questions.a: The arrangement of atoms, bonds and chains in a material directly controls its physical and chemical properties — so different bonding structures give different melting points, strengths and conductivities.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the repeat unit of poly(ethene)?
flashcard_questions.a: –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ– The double bond in ethene (CH₂=CH₂) opens and the monomers join in a long chain.

glossary_terms.definition: A very large molecule made by joining many small molecules (monomers) together in a long chain. The repeating unit in the chain is structurally identical to the monomer.
A small molecule that can join with many others to form a polymer chain. Monomers for addition polymers must have a C=C bond; monomers for condensation polymers must have two functional groups.
Polymerisation in which alkene monomers open their C=C double bond and join together in a chain, with no by-product formed.
Polymerisation in which monomers with two different functional groups react together, releasing a small molecule (usually water) at each bond formed.
Polyethylene terephthalate — a polyester made from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid by condensation polymerisation. Used in drinks bottles and polyester fibres.
A polymer whose chains are held by weak intermolecular forces. It softens when heated and can be remoulded and recycled. Also called a thermoplastic.
A polymer whose chains are joined by permanent covalent cross-links. It cannot soften on heating, so it cannot be recycled — it chars instead of melting.
An organic compound with two carboxylic acid (–COOH) groups. It reacts with a diol in condensation polymerisation to form a polyester, releasing water at each linkage.
